title: Periodic motion
subject: physics
definition:
Periodic motion is a type of motion in which an object repeats the same movement again and again after a fixed, equal interval of time. The key idea is the word "fixed" -- every repetition must occur after exactly the same duration, not a shorter or longer one. A simple pendulum is the classic example: when a small heavy ball called the bob is pulled to one side and released, it swings to and fro, passing through the centre each time and reaching the same height on the other side. Because each complete swing takes the same amount of time, the pendulum's motion is periodic. This is why pendulum clocks were used for centuries to keep time -- the regular, repeating swing of the bob drives the hands of the clock forward at a steady rate.

Closely related is oscillatory motion, which is a special kind of periodic motion in which an object moves to and fro about a fixed point or mean position. A swing in a park, the vibrating string of a sitar, the prongs of a tuning fork, and a child on a jhoola during a festival are all examples of oscillatory motion. Every oscillatory motion is periodic, because each to-and-fro swing takes the same time, but not every periodic motion is oscillatory -- the minute hand of a clock repeats its motion every sixty minutes but does not move to and fro, so it is periodic without being oscillatory.

Repetitive motion is the broader family: any motion that happens again and again is repetitive. Within repetitive motion we distinguish two groups. If the repetitions occur after equal time intervals, the motion is periodic. If the repetitions occur after unequal, changing time intervals, the motion is non-periodic. A bouncing ball dropped on the floor is a good example of non-periodic motion: it bounces again and again, so the motion is repetitive, but after each bounce it rises to a smaller height and the time between successive bounces keeps decreasing. A vehicle braking to a stop in heavy traffic on a Mumbai road, or a fan switched off and slowing down, are also non-periodic because the intervals between similar events change. The earth rotating on its axis to produce day and night is periodic, because each rotation takes roughly 24 hours -- the same interval every time.

To decide whether a motion is periodic or non-periodic, ask two questions: first, does the object repeat its motion at all? If yes, the motion is repetitive. Second, are the time intervals between repetitions equal? If equal, it is periodic; if not, it is non-periodic. The fixed interval after which the motion repeats is called the time interval of the periodic motion. At this stage we only identify and describe periodic motion qualitatively; measuring the time period and frequency in seconds and hertz is reserved for Class 7.
eli5: Think of a swing in a park. It goes forward and back, forward and back, and each full swing takes the same time -- that is periodic motion, because it repeats after a fixed time. Now think of a ball you drop: it bounces, but each bounce is smaller and quicker than the last, so the time keeps changing -- that is non-periodic motion. Periodic means "same time, again and again."

misconceptions.belief: Any motion that repeats is periodic.
misconceptions.correction: Repeating motion is only repetitive; it becomes periodic only when the repetitions happen after equal, fixed time intervals. CISCE examiners have repeatedly flagged rote learning and confusion between similar terms -- students write "periodic = repeats" without the "fixed interval" condition. A bouncing ball repeats but with shorter and shorter intervals, so it is repetitive but non-periodic, not periodic.

misconceptions.belief: Periodic motion and oscillatory motion are the same thing.
misconceptions.correction: Every oscillatory motion is periodic, but not every periodic motion is oscillatory. Oscillatory motion must be a to-and-fro movement about a fixed mean position (pendulum, swing, tuning fork). The minute hand of a clock is periodic -- it repeats every 60 minutes -- but it is not oscillatory because it goes round in one direction, not to and fro. Examiners have observed that candidates confuse closely related technical terms, so this distinction matters.

misconceptions.belief: A pendulum eventually stops, so it is non-periodic.
misconceptions.correction: A real pendulum does slow down due to air resistance and friction at the support, but while it is swinging freely each oscillation still takes almost the same time -- the time interval stays nearly constant even as the height decreases. The motion is therefore still treated as periodic in this introductory study. Non-periodic refers to changing time intervals between repetitions, not to the motion dying out.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Define periodic motion and give two examples from everyday life.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: Periodic motion is the motion of an object that repeats itself after a fixed, equal interval of time. The two essential features are that the motion repeats, and that the time between successive repetitions is the same. Two everyday examples are: (1) a simple pendulum -- when the bob is pulled to one side and released, it swings to and fro, and each complete swing takes the same amount of time; and (2) the minute hand of a clock, which returns to the same position on the dial every sixty minutes. Both repeat their motion after a fixed interval, so both are periodic. A swing in a park is another good example: each complete to-and-fro swing takes the same time, making the motion periodic as well as oscillatory.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A ball is dropped on the floor and bounces several times. A student says this is periodic motion because the ball bounces again and again. Explain why the student is wrong.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The student is confusing repetitive motion with periodic motion. It is true that the bouncing ball repeats its motion -- it bounces up and falls down many times -- so the motion is repetitive. However, periodic motion requires the repetition to occur after a fixed, equal interval of time. In the case of a dropped ball, each bounce is smaller than the previous one because some energy is lost to the floor and to air resistance at every impact. As the bounce height decreases, the time between successive bounces also becomes shorter and shorter. Because the time intervals are not equal but keep changing, the motion is non-periodic, not periodic. The correct classification is: the bouncing ball shows repetitive but non-periodic motion. This example highlights why the phrase "fixed interval of time" is the heart of the definition of periodic motion and cannot be ignored.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A classmate claims that the motion of the minute hand of a clock is oscillatory motion because it repeats regularly. Evaluate this claim and give a balanced judgement.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The classmate is partly right and partly wrong, and the error is an important one. The part that is correct is that the minute hand's motion is indeed periodic: it returns to the same position on the dial after a fixed interval of sixty minutes, so it satisfies both conditions for periodic motion -- repetition and a fixed time interval. However, the claim that it is oscillatory is incorrect. Oscillatory motion is a specific kind of periodic motion in which the object moves to and fro about a fixed mean position. Examples of truly oscillatory motion are a pendulum bob swinging left and right about its rest position, a child on a swing moving forward and back about the lowest point, and the prongs of a tuning fork vibrating about their rest position. In every one of these cases the body reverses its direction repeatedly and passes through a central mean position. The minute hand of a clock does none of this: it moves continuously in one direction around the dial and never reverses, never moves to and fro, and has no mean position about which it oscillates. Therefore the minute hand is periodic but not oscillatory. The balanced judgement is: the classmate correctly identified the motion as periodic but wrongly labelled it oscillatory. The correct statement is, "The minute hand of a clock shows periodic motion but not oscillatory motion, because it repeats at a fixed interval but does not move to and fro about a mean position." This distinction -- that every oscillatory motion is periodic but not every periodic motion is oscillatory -- is exactly the kind of precise use of terms that CISCE examiners expect, and they have repeatedly cautioned against rote learning and the loose use of technical vocabulary.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Identify whether each of the following is periodic, non-periodic, or not repetitive, and give a one-line reason: (a) the earth rotating on its axis, (b) a car moving through crowded traffic stopping and starting, (c) a stone dropped into a well, (d) a vibrating string of a sitar.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: (a) The earth rotating on its axis is periodic motion, because each complete rotation takes roughly the same fixed time -- about 24 hours -- producing day and night at regular intervals. (b) A car moving through crowded traffic, stopping and starting, is non-periodic motion: the motion repeats in a loose sense (stop, go, stop, go) but the time intervals between stops and starts vary constantly depending on the traffic, so the intervals are not fixed. (c) A stone dropped into a well is not repetitive motion at all -- it falls once and does not repeat its movement, so it is neither periodic nor non-periodic; it is simply one-way motion under gravity. (d) A vibrating string of a sitar is periodic and also oscillatory motion, because the string moves to and fro about its rest position and each vibration takes the same fixed time, producing a steady musical note. The reasoning in each case follows the two-step test: first ask whether the motion repeats, then ask whether the time intervals between repetitions are equal.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Design a simple experiment using a pendulum you can make at home to demonstrate periodic motion to a younger sibling. Describe what you would use, what you would do, and how you would convince them that the motion is periodic.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: To demonstrate periodic motion, I would make a simple pendulum at home. I would take a small, heavy object such as a metal washer or a rubber eraser to act as the bob, and tie it to the end of a piece of cotton thread about one metre long. I would tie the other end of the thread to a fixed support such as the edge of a table or a hook on a wall, so that the bob hangs freely. I would then pull the bob a small distance to one side -- only a few centimetres, so the swing stays gentle -- and release it without pushing, letting it swing freely. To convince my younger sibling that the motion is periodic, I would use a stopwatch or a phone timer and measure the time for ten complete to-and-fro swings, then divide by ten to find the time for one swing. I would repeat this measurement two or three times and show that the time for one swing comes out almost the same each time -- for example, about two seconds. I would explain that because each swing takes the same fixed time, the motion is periodic. I would also point out that the bob moves to and fro about the central rest position, so the motion is also oscillatory. Finally, I would contrast it with a ball dropped on the floor, whose bounces get faster and faster, to show the difference between periodic and non-periodic motion.

masteryCriteria: Can define periodic motion as motion that repeats after a fixed, equal interval of time; can distinguish periodic from non-periodic motion using the "equal interval" test (e.g., pendulum = periodic, bouncing ball = non-periodic); can give at least three examples of periodic motion (pendulum bob, swing, minute hand of a clock); can explain that every oscillatory motion is periodic but not every periodic motion is oscillatory, using the minute hand as the counter-example.

title: Uniform and non-uniform motion
subject: physics
definition:
Motion, as you already know, is the change in the position of an object with time. When an object moves along a straight line, we call it rectilinear motion. Now we take that idea one step further and ask a sharper question: does the object cover the same distance in every equal chunk of time, or does the distance keep changing? The answer splits all motion into two neat families -- uniform motion and non-uniform motion.

Uniform motion is defined as the motion of an object when it travels equal distances in equal intervals of time. The key word is "equal intervals" -- meaning any chunks of time of the same size, such as every one second, every five minutes, or every one hour. If, in each of those equal chunks, the object covers exactly the same distance, the motion is uniform. A car on cruise control travelling on a straight highway at a steady 60 km/h is a textbook example: in every one minute it covers exactly one kilometre, in every hour it covers exactly sixty kilometres. A ceiling fan rotating at a constant speed is another example, because the tip of each blade sweeps through the same arc in every equal time interval, just like the hand of a clock sweeping smoothly. A train running non-stop on a straight, level track at a steady speed, or an athlete jogging at a perfectly steady pace around a circular track, also show uniform motion.

Non-uniform motion is the motion of an object when it travels unequal distances in equal intervals of time. Here the distance covered in each equal chunk of time is different -- sometimes more, sometimes less, sometimes zero. A bus stopping at traffic lights on a busy city road is the classic daily-life example: it speeds up, slows down, halts, and starts again, so the distance it covers in each one-minute interval keeps changing. A ball rolling down a sloping track speeds up continuously, so it covers more distance in each successive second -- that too is non-uniform motion. A rickshaw winding through narrow Indian streets, a child on a swing, and a car braking to a stop are all non-uniform because the distance per equal time interval is not constant.

The practical test is simple: pick equal time intervals (say, every 5 seconds), measure the distance covered in each, and compare. Equal distances mean uniform; unequal distances mean non-uniform. Most real-life motion around us -- walking, cycling in traffic, a train pulling out of a station -- is non-uniform. Truly uniform motion is rare and usually happens only under controlled conditions, which is why it is treated as a special, idealised case. This distinction is the foundation on which the later ideas of speed, velocity, and acceleration are built, but at this stage we focus only on recognising and classifying the two types using the equal-distance-in-equal-time rule.
eli5: Think of a ticking clock and a hopping frog. The clock's second hand sweeps the same little arc every second -- equal distance every equal second -- that is uniform motion. The frog hops, sits, hops again -- sometimes far, sometimes near, sometimes not at all in the same second -- unequal distances in equal time -- that is non-uniform motion. Same time chunks, same distance each time means uniform; different distances means non-uniform.

misconceptions.belief: A fast object is in uniform motion; a slow object is in non-uniform motion.
misconceptions.correction: Speed has nothing to do with the uniform/non-uniform split. A slow train crawling at a steady 20 km/h along a straight track is in uniform motion because it covers equal distances in equal intervals. A fast motorcycle zig-zagging and braking through traffic is in non-uniform motion because the distance per equal interval keeps changing. The test is equality of distance in equal time, not how fast or slow the object is.

misconceptions.belief: Uniform motion means moving in a straight line only.
misconceptions.correction:
Rectilinear motion (node c6_phy_008) is about the shape of the path; uniform motion is about the steadiness of distance covered in equal time. A ceiling fan blade tip moving in a circle at constant speed covers equal arc lengths in equal seconds, so it is uniform motion even though the path is not straight. The two ideas are related but not the same.

Misconception 3 (grounded in CISCE examiner observations): Examiners in the 2024 and 2025 Pupil Performance Analysis noted that many candidates "were not clear with the concept" and used "guesswork" instead of relating the concept to daily-life examples, and they reminded teachers to "express every physical quantity with proper unit" and "demonstrate the concepts in the class by showing it to the students." Students often answer "the bus is non-uniform" without stating the equal interval or the unequal distances. Correction: Always state the interval (e.g. "every 1 minute"), give at least two distances (e.g. "300 m then 50 m then 0 m"), and only then conclude. Vague answers without units or numbers lose marks even when the final label is correct.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Define uniform motion and non-uniform motion in your own words.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: Uniform motion is the motion of an object that travels equal distances in equal intervals of time. For example, if a car covers exactly 1 km in every 1 minute, again and again, the distances in each equal one-minute interval are the same, so the motion is uniform. Non-uniform motion is the motion of an object that travels unequal distances in equal intervals of time. For example, if a bus covers 300 m in the first minute, 50 m in the second minute, and 0 m in the third minute while waiting at a red light, the distances in equal one-minute intervals are different, so the motion is non-uniform. The deciding rule is always the same: pick equal time intervals, measure the distance in each, and compare. Equal distances mean uniform; unequal distances mean non-uniform. The size of the interval does not matter as long as the intervals themselves are equal, and the speed of the object does not matter -- only the steadiness of the distance covered per equal interval.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A train moves on a straight track. In four successive 10-second intervals it covers 50 m, 50 m, 50 m, and 50 m. A car on a city road in four successive 10-second intervals covers 80 m, 20 m, 0 m, and 60 m. Classify each and explain your reasoning.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The train is in uniform motion because it covers equal distances (50 m) in each of the four equal 10-second intervals. The distances are identical in every equal time chunk, which is exactly the condition for uniform motion. The car is in non-uniform motion because the distances it covers in the same equal 10-second intervals are unequal -- 80 m, then 20 m, then 0 m (it stopped), then 60 m. Because at least one interval gives a different distance, the motion fails the equal-distance-in-equal-time test and is therefore non-uniform. Notice that we did not need to calculate speed; we only needed to compare distances across equal intervals. Also notice that the train could be slow or fast and still be uniform -- what matters is the equality of the distances, not their size. The car's stopping (0 m in one interval) is a clear sign of non-uniform motion, since a uniform-motion object never stops within the chosen intervals.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A student says, "A ceiling fan rotating at constant speed is in non-uniform motion because it is not moving in a straight line -- it goes round and round." Evaluate this statement. Is the student correct? Give a balanced argument and state your final judgement.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The student's statement is incorrect, and the error lies in confusing the shape of the path with the rule for uniform motion. The definition of uniform motion does not require a straight-line path; it requires that the object cover equal distances in equal intervals of time. The path can be straight, circular, or any other shape -- the test is always about distance covered per equal time interval, not about the geometry of the path. Consider the tip of a ceiling fan blade rotating at constant speed. In every one second it sweeps through the same arc length along its circular path, because the fan turns at a steady rate. So in each equal one-second interval the tip covers exactly the same distance, which satisfies the definition of uniform motion. It is true that rectilinear motion (node c6_phy_008), which the student studied earlier, is motion along a straight line, and many uniform-motion examples in the textbook are also rectilinear. That overlap is probably what leads the student to think uniform motion must be straight-line motion. But the two ideas are different: rectilinear motion describes the path, whereas uniform motion describes the steadiness of distance in equal time. A fan blade tip is not in rectilinear motion, yet it is in uniform motion. Conversely, a car on a straight road that keeps braking and accelerating is in rectilinear motion but non-uniform motion. So path shape and uniformity are independent ideas. Final judgement: the student is wrong. The ceiling fan at constant speed is in uniform motion because it covers equal distances (equal arc lengths) in equal intervals of time, regardless of the circular path.

diagnosticQuestions.question: You observe a rickshaw on an Indian street for 5 seconds. You record its position at the end of each second and find it has covered 4 m, 6 m, 2 m, 8 m, and 1 m in the five one-second intervals. Classify the motion and justify your answer with the data.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The rickshaw is in non-uniform motion. The five time intervals are equal -- each is one second -- but the distances covered in them are unequal: 4 m in the first second, 6 m in the second, 2 m in the third, 8 m in the fourth, and 1 m in the fifth. Because the distance changes from interval to interval (4, then 6, then 2, then 8, then 1), the equal-distance-in-equal-time condition is broken, so the motion is non-uniform. This matches everyday experience: a rickshaw in traffic speeds up, slows down, dodges obstacles, and stops, so it cannot cover the same distance in every second. To classify motion in this way, always follow three steps: choose equal time intervals, record the distance for each interval, and compare the distances. If they are all equal, label the motion uniform; if even one differs, label it non-uniform. Stating the actual distances with units (metres, seconds) is essential -- examiners in the CISCE Pupil Performance Analysis repeatedly remind students to express every physical quantity with a proper unit.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Design a simple classroom experiment using a marble, a long ruler marked in centimetres, and a stopwatch to demonstrate both uniform and non-uniform motion to a friend. Describe what you would do, what you would measure, and how you would use the results to show the difference.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: I would set up two tracks using the long ruler. For the first demonstration, I would place the ruler flat on a smooth, level table so the marble rolls at a steady, slow speed after a gentle push. I would mark the marble's position every 1 second for 5 seconds using the stopwatch and read off the distance covered in each one-second interval from the centimre markings. If the marble covers, say, 10 cm, 10 cm, 10 cm, 10 cm, and 10 cm in the five equal seconds, I would tell my friend: "Equal distances in equal intervals -- this is uniform motion." For the second demonstration, I would tilt the ruler by lifting one end so the marble rolls down and speeds up. Again I would mark the position every 1 second for 5 seconds. This time the distances would increase -- perhaps 5 cm, 10 cm, 15 cm, 20 cm, 25 cm -- because the marble accelerates down the slope. I would tell my friend: "Unequal distances in equal intervals -- this is non-uniform motion." By keeping the time intervals equal (1 second each) in both cases and only changing the track, I isolate distance as the variable that decides the type of motion. I would finish by asking my friend to predict what the distances would look like if I pushed the marble so it slowed down and stopped -- increasing then decreasing then zero -- reinforcing that any set of unequal distances in equal time means non-uniform motion.

masteryCriteria: Can define uniform motion in own words as "an object travels equal distances in equal intervals of time" and give a daily-life example (e.g. a car on cruise control covering exactly 1 km every 1 minute); can define non-uniform motion in own words as "an object travels unequal distances in equal intervals of time" and give a daily-life example (e.g. a bus at traffic lights covering 300 m, then 50 m, then 0 m in successive one-minute intervals); can classify a given motion example as uniform or non-uniform by checking whether distances in equal time intervals are equal or unequal; can state that the size of the time interval does not matter as long as the intervals are equal.

title: Speed and average speed
subject: physics
definition:
Speed is a measure of how fast an object moves. It is defined as the ratio of the total distance travelled by an object to the total time taken to travel that distance. In symbols, speed = total distance / total time. The SI unit of speed is the metre per second, written as m/s (sometimes m s^-1). A commonly used larger unit is the kilometre per hour, written as km/h. The two units are related by a fixed conversion factor: 1 m/s = 3.6 km/h, and 1 km/h = 5/18 m/s (approximately 0.278 m/s). For example, a car covering 120 metres in 10 seconds has a speed of 120 / 10 = 12 m/s, which is the same as 12 x 3.6 = 43.2 km/h.

When an object moves with uniform motion -- covering equal distances in equal intervals of time -- its speed stays the same throughout, and we call it simply the speed of the object. However, most real journeys are non-uniform: a bus stopping at traffic signals, a runner slowing on a slope, or a cyclist speeding downhill. For such journeys the speed keeps changing, so a single value of "speed" does not describe the whole trip. We then use the idea of average speed. Average speed is defined as the total distance travelled divided by the total time taken for the entire journey. The formula is average speed = total distance / total time, and it is expressed in the same units, m/s or km/h.

Average speed is not the simple average (arithmetic mean) of the individual speeds. It is a ratio of two totals. For example, if a scooter travels 30 km in the first hour at 30 km/h and then 60 km in the next two hours at 30 km/h, the average speed is (30 + 60) km / (1 + 2) h = 90 km / 3 h = 30 km/h. But if it travels 30 km in 1 hour and then 30 km in 2 hours, the average speed is (30 + 30) / (1 + 2) = 60 / 3 = 20 km/h -- not the mean of 30 and 15. This distinction is the heart of the concept: average speed summarises the whole journey as a single number, even though some parts were faster and some slower, just as a report card summarises a term's performance even though individual tests varied.

In ICSE Class 6, students are expected to define speed and average speed, write the correct formula, substitute given values of distance and time, perform the division, and write the answer with the correct unit. They should also convert between m/s and km/h using the factors 3.6 and 5/18. Numerical questions typically give a journey split into two or three legs with different distances and times, and ask for the average speed over the whole journey. The unit must always be written with the final answer -- a number without a unit is incomplete.
eli5: Speed is like a scorecard for a runner -- it tells you how much distance was covered in each unit of time. Average speed is like the average marks on a report card: it summarises the whole journey even though some parts were faster and some slower. To find it, divide the total distance by the total time, and always write the unit (m/s or km/h) with your answer.

misconceptions.belief: Average speed is the arithmetic mean of the individual speeds.
misconceptions.correction: Average speed is total distance divided by total time, NOT the simple average of the speeds. CISCE examiners (PPA 2020, Q4) repeatedly flagged incorrect substitution in numericals -- students plug in speeds instead of distances and times. The correct method is to add up all the distances for the numerator and all the times (including stops) for the denominator, then divide.

misconceptions.belief: The unit does not matter as long as the number is right.
misconceptions.correction: CISCE examiners (PPA 2020, Q4) explicitly noted "Units were not written in the final answer" as a common error. A numerical answer without the correct unit (m/s or km/h) is incomplete and loses marks. Always state the unit, and make sure it matches the data -- if distance is in km and time in hours, the answer is in km/h, not m/s.

misconceptions.belief: Stoppage or rest time should be ignored because the object was not moving.
misconceptions.correction: Average speed describes the whole journey, including stops. The total time in the denominator must include every minute from start to finish, whether the object was moving or resting. Ignoring stop time inflates the average speed and gives a wrong answer.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Define speed and average speed, and state the SI unit of speed.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: Speed is defined as the ratio of the total distance travelled by an object to the total time taken to travel that distance; in symbols, speed = total distance / total time. When the motion is uniform, this ratio gives a single constant value called the speed of the object. When the motion is non-uniform, the speed keeps changing from one instant to another, so we use average speed instead -- average speed is defined as the total distance travelled during the entire journey divided by the total time taken for the entire journey, including any stops. The formula is the same in form: average speed = total distance / total time. The SI unit of speed is the metre per second, written as m/s (or m s^-1). A commonly used larger unit is the kilometre per hour, km/h, related to m/s by the factors 1 m/s = 3.6 km/h and 1 km/h = 5/18 m/s. Both units are acceptable, but the unit chosen must match the data given in the question, and the unit must always be written with the final numerical answer.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A cyclist travels 6 km in 20 minutes and then a further 4 km in 10 minutes. Explain why the average speed is not simply the average of the two speeds, and calculate the correct average speed in km/h.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The two legs have speeds of 6 km / (20/60) h = 18 km/h and 4 km / (10/60) h = 24 km/h. The arithmetic mean of these two speeds is (18 + 24)/2 = 21 km/h, but this is NOT the average speed, because the two legs took different lengths of time. Average speed is defined as total distance divided by total time, not as the mean of the speeds. The total distance is 6 + 4 = 10 km. The total time is 20 min + 10 min = 30 min = 0.5 h. Therefore the average speed = 10 km / 0.5 h = 20 km/h, which is different from 21 km/h. The reason is that the slower leg (18 km/h) lasted twice as long as the faster leg (24 km/h), so it weighs more heavily in the true average. This is exactly why we must use the ratio of totals and never the simple mean of speeds -- a point CISCE examiners have flagged when students make incorrect substitutions in numerical problems.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A student says, "If a bus travels the first half of a distance at 40 km/h and the second half at 60 km/h, the average speed for the whole journey is 50 km/h, because 50 is exactly halfway between 40 and 60." Evaluate this claim.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The claim is incorrect, and it is a very common error. The student is computing the arithmetic mean of the two speeds, but average speed is defined as total distance divided by total time -- not the mean of the speeds. Let us check with numbers. Suppose the total distance is 120 km, so each half is 60 km. The first half at 40 km/h takes 60/40 = 1.5 h. The second half at 60 km/h takes 60/60 = 1.0 h. The total time is therefore 1.5 + 1.0 = 2.5 h. The average speed = total distance / total time = 120 km / 2.5 h = 48 km/h, not 50 km/h. The reason the true average is less than 50 km/h is that the bus spent more time travelling at the slower speed (1.5 h) than at the faster speed (1.0 h). The slower portion therefore dominates the time-averaged value and pulls the average down. In general, when equal distances are travelled at two different speeds u and v, the average speed is the harmonic mean 2uv/(u + v), not the arithmetic mean (u + v)/2. For u = 40 and v = 60, this gives 2 x 40 x 60 / (40 + 60) = 4800/100 = 48 km/h, confirming our calculation. The student's reasoning fails because it ignores the time spent at each speed; only the ratio of total distance to total time gives the correct average speed. This is precisely the kind of error CISCE examiners flag when they warn about "incorrect substitution" and "wrong formula" in numerical answers.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A train travels 150 km in 2.5 hours, stops at a station for 30 minutes, and then travels 90 km in 1.5 hours. Calculate the average speed for the entire journey in (a) km/h and (b) m/s.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: First identify the total distance and the total time, remembering that the stop counts as part of the total time. Total distance = 150 km + 90 km = 240 km. Total time = 2.5 h + 0.5 h (stop) + 1.5 h = 4.5 h. (a) Average speed in km/h = total distance / total time = 240 km / 4.5 h = 53.33 km/h (to two decimal places). (b) To convert km/h to m/s, multiply by 5/18: 53.33 x 5/18 = 14.81 m/s (approximately). So the average speed is about 53.33 km/h, or about 14.81 m/s. Note the working: the formula was written, the values were substituted with their units, the stop time was included in the total time, and the final answers carry the correct units in both systems. This is the format expected in the ICSE board examination.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Design a short journey for a delivery scooter in an Indian city that has two legs with different speeds and a stop, and write a full worked solution for its average speed. Include the formula, the substitution, and the unit conversion from km/h to m/s.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: Consider a delivery scooter in Delhi. It travels 12 km from a restaurant in Connaught Place to a customer in Karol Bagh in 30 minutes, waits 10 minutes at the customer's gate, and then travels 8 km to a second customer in Rajendra Nagar in 20 minutes. Total distance = 12 + 8 = 20 km. Total time = 30 min + 10 min + 20 min = 60 min = 1 h. Average speed = total distance / total time = 20 km / 1 h = 20 km/h. To convert to m/s: 20 x 5/18 = 100/18 = 5.56 m/s (approximately). So the scooter's average speed for the whole delivery run is 20 km/h, or about 5.56 m/s. The worked solution shows the formula (average speed = total distance / total time), the substitution with all distances and times including the wait, the division giving 20 km/h, and the unit conversion using the factor 5/18 to reach m/s. A student who presents the answer this way -- formula, substitution, computation, correct unit, and conversion -- meets the full expectation of the ICSE board for a numerical on average speed.

masteryCriteria: Can define speed and average speed as total distance divided by total time and write the formula speed = total distance / total time; can calculate average speed from given distance and time data (e.g. 240 km in 4.5 h = 53.3 km/h) including journeys with stops; can convert between m/s and km/h using the factors 3.6 and 5/18 (e.g. 20 m/s = 72 km/h, 72 km/h = 20 m/s); can explain why average speed is not the arithmetic mean of the individual speeds.

title: Force as a push or pull that changes state of motion
subject: physics
definition:
A force is a push or a pull exerted on an object. It is an interaction between two bodies -- the one applying the force and the one on which the force is applied -- and it cannot be seen directly; we infer its presence from the effects it produces. The two elementary kinds of force that a Class 6 student meets are a push (when you drive something away from you, such as pushing a door open or pushing a stationary football) and a pull (when you draw something towards you, such as pulling a drawer or pulling a rope in a tug-of-war). Both are forces; the words push and pull only describe the direction in which the force acts relative to the person applying it.

The most important effect of a force, and the focus of this node, is that it can change the state of motion of an object. The state of motion of a body is described by whether it is stationary or moving and, if it is moving, by how fast (its speed) and in which direction it travels. A force can therefore produce five observable changes: (i) it can start a stationary object moving -- for example, a child kicks a football at rest and the ball begins to roll; (ii) it can stop a moving object -- a fielder catches a cricket ball and the pull of the hands brings it to rest; (iii) it can speed up a moving object -- a cyclist pedals harder and the bicycle accelerates; (iv) it can slow down a moving object -- a driver applies the brakes and the car decelerates; and (v) it can change the direction of a moving object -- a batsman hits a cricket ball and it flies off in a new direction, or a hockey player deflects a pass. Starting and stopping are special cases of changing speed (from zero to some value, or from some value to zero), and speeding up and slowing down are called acceleration and deceleration respectively.

A force can also change the shape of an object, even when the object does not move as a whole. Squeezing a rubber ball, pressing a sponge, stretching a rubber band, kneading clay, or pressing a lump of dough between the palms all show that a force can deform a body. In some materials (such as a rubber band or a sponge) the shape is recovered when the force is removed, while in others (such as clay or dough) the new shape is retained.

The activity prescribed in the syllabus makes all these effects visible: push a stationary ball to start it rolling, stop a rolling ball with your hand, squeeze a sponge, and stretch a rubber band. From these simple acts a Class 6 student concludes that a force is recognised by its effects -- changing the state of motion (starting, stopping, speeding up, slowing down, changing direction) and changing the shape of an object.
eli5: A force is just a push or a pull. Think of a football lying still on the ground -- it is not going anywhere. When you kick it, your foot pushes it and it starts rolling. When you catch it, your hands pull it and it stops. If you pedal harder on your cycle it goes faster; if you press the brakes it goes slower; if you tap a moving ball sideways it turns. You can also squeeze a sponge or stretch a rubber band and watch its shape change. So a force is recognised by what it does -- it starts, stops, speeds up, slows down, turns, or reshapes things.

misconceptions.belief: A stationary object has no force acting on it." The CISCE examiner reports that many candidates believe an object at rest is free of force and that only a moving body experiences force.
misconceptions.correction: A book lying on a table is stationary, but gravity pulls it downwards and the table pushes it upwards; these forces balance and the book stays at rest. At Class 6 we only need to recognise that a stationary object can have forces acting on it -- the detailed idea of balanced forces is reserved for Class 7. The key point for this node is that a force is needed to change the state of rest, not that no force acts on a body at rest.

misconceptions.belief: Force is always a push; a pull is something different." Some candidates treat push and pull as two separate physical quantities.
misconceptions.correction: Push and pull are both forces -- they differ only in the direction in which the force is applied relative to the person. Pulling a rope towards you and pushing a ball away from you are both forces; the words describe direction, not kind.

misconceptions.belief: Force changes shape only in soft objects, so hard objects like a steel spoon are not affected by force." The examiner notes that candidates often ignore shape change in rigid bodies.
misconceptions.correction: Any object can have its shape changed by a sufficiently large force -- even a steel rod bends under a big enough load. In Class 6 we use soft examples (sponge, rubber band, clay) because the change is easy to see, but the principle applies to all materials; the amount of change depends on the strength of the force and the material.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Define force and list the five effects it can have on the state of motion of an object, with one example each.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: A force is a push or a pull exerted on a body by another body. It is recognised by the effects it produces. The five effects of force on the state of motion are: (i) starting a stationary object -- kicking a stationary football makes it roll; (ii) stopping a moving object -- a fielder catches a moving cricket ball and the pull of the hands brings it to rest; (iii) speeding up a moving object -- a cyclist pedals harder and the bicycle accelerates from 5 m/s to 8 m/s; (iv) slowing down a moving object -- applying the brakes decelerates a moving car from 30 km/h to 10 km/h; and (v) changing the direction of a moving object -- a batsman hits a cricket ball and it flies off in a new direction towards the boundary. In every case the force changes the state of motion, which is described by whether the body is stationary or moving and, if moving, by its speed and direction.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A child rolls a ball along the floor and then places a hand flat in front of it. The ball stops. Explain which force acted, in which direction, and how the state of motion changed from before to after.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: Before the hand is placed, the ball is moving -- its state of motion is "moving with a certain speed in a particular direction along the floor". When the child places a flat hand in front of the ball, the hand exerts a push (a force) on the ball. The direction of this push is opposite to the direction in which the ball is rolling. This opposing force acts on the moving ball and reduces its speed step by step until the speed becomes zero. So the state of motion changes from "moving" to "stationary". The force here is a push applied by the hand, acting against the direction of motion, and its effect is to stop the ball. This is an example of force decelerating a body to rest. A good answer names the force (push by the hand), its direction (opposite to motion), and the before-and-after states (moving to stationary), which is exactly what the board examiner looks for.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A student writes, "A force can only change the state of motion of an object; it cannot change anything else." Evaluate this statement and correct it using examples from the syllabus.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The statement is incorrect and incomplete. While changing the state of motion is one of the most important effects of force, it is not the only effect. A force can also change the shape of an object, and in some situations it can change the direction of a moving body without changing its speed. The syllabus explicitly lists shape change as an effect of force: squeezing a rubber ball flattens it temporarily, pressing a sponge compresses it, stretching a rubber band elongates it, and kneading clay or dough gives it a new shape that may be permanent. In each of these cases the body as a whole may not move from one place to another, yet a clear change has occurred -- the shape has changed because of the applied force. Therefore the correct statement is: "A force can change the state of motion of an object (by starting it, stopping it, speeding it up, slowing it down, or changing its direction) and it can also change the shape of an object." A balanced evaluation would add that in many real situations both effects can happen together -- for example, when a batsman hits a cricket ball, the bat both changes the ball's direction of motion and, very slightly, changes its shape for an instant. Ignoring the shape effect, as the student has done, would lose marks in a board question that asks for "two effects of force", because the examiner expects both the motion effect and the shape effect to be mentioned. The CISCE pupil performance analysis repeatedly warns that candidates who give only one category of effect score partially, so a complete answer must cover both motion and shape.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Carry out the syllabus activity -- push a stationary ball, stop a rolling ball, squeeze a sponge, and stretch a rubber band. For each action, record (a) the type of force applied (push or pull), (b) the object acted upon, and (c) the observed effect on state of motion or shape.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: Action 1 -- Push a stationary ball: (a) a push is applied by the hand or foot; (b) the object is the ball at rest on the ground; (c) the state of motion changes from stationary to moving -- the ball starts rolling. Action 2 -- Stop a rolling ball: (a) a push is applied by the hand placed in front of the ball, acting opposite to the direction of rolling; (b) the object is the moving ball; (c) the state of motion changes from moving to stationary -- the ball comes to rest. Action 3 -- Squeeze a sponge: (a) a push is applied by the fingers and palm pressing inward from both sides; (b) the object is the sponge; (c) the shape of the sponge changes -- it is compressed, and it regains its shape when the force is removed. Action 4 -- Stretch a rubber band: (a) a pull is applied by both hands pulling the ends outward; (b) the object is the rubber band; (c) the shape of the rubber band changes -- it elongates, and it returns to its original length when released. This table of observations shows that force is recognised by its effects on motion (start, stop) and on shape (compress, elongate), which is the core conclusion of this node.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Design a simple classroom demonstration using only objects found at home that shows all five effects of force on the state of motion plus one shape change. Describe each step, the force used, and what the audience should observe.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: I would use a small rubber ball, a smooth floor, a wall, and a sponge. Step 1 (Start): Place the rubber ball at rest on the floor and gently push it with one finger. The audience observes a stationary ball begin to roll -- force has started its motion. Step 2 (Speed up): While the ball is rolling slowly, give it a second, stronger push in the same direction. The audience sees the ball move faster -- force has accelerated it. Step 3 (Change direction): Aim the rolling ball so that it strikes a wall at an angle; the audience watches it bounce off in a new direction -- force from the wall has changed the direction of motion. Step 4 (Slow down): Let the ball roll onto a rough mat or a carpet; the audience observes it gradually slow down -- the frictional force of the rough surface has decelerated it. Step 5 (Stop): Place a hand or a book in the ball's path; the audience sees the ball come to rest -- the push from the hand has stopped it. Step 6 (Shape change): Finally, hand the sponge to a volunteer and ask them to squeeze it; the audience sees the sponge compress and then spring back -- force has changed its shape. The demonstration closes by asking the audience to name, for each step, whether the effect was on the state of motion (start, speed up, change direction, slow down, stop) or on the shape (compress). This single set of household objects thus displays every effect of force listed in the syllabus and gives a Class 6 student a memorable, hands-on summary of the whole node.

masteryCriteria: Can define force as a push or pull in own words and distinguish a push from a pull by the direction in which the force acts; can state the five effects of force on the state of motion (start a stationary object, stop a moving object, speed up/accelerate, slow down/decelerate, change direction) with one concrete example each, such as kicking a stationary football to start it and a fielder catching a cricket ball to stop it; can give at least two examples of force changing the shape of an object (squeezing a sponge, stretching a rubber band, kneading clay); can describe a simple activity (push a stationary ball, stop a rolling ball, squeeze a sponge, stretch a rubber band) and correctly record the force type, the object, and the observed effect on motion or shape.

title: Types of forces (contact and non-contact)
subject: physics
definition:
A force is a push or a pull that can change the state of motion or the shape of an object. Forces can be classified into two broad categories based on whether the two interacting bodies need to be in physical contact with each other. This classification produces contact forces and non-contact forces. A contact force is one in which the two interacting bodies must touch each other for the force to act. The two important contact forces studied at this level are muscular force and frictional force. Muscular force is the force applied by the muscles of humans or animals when they push, pull, lift, kick, or squeeze an object -- for example, a boy pushing a heavy box across the floor, a bullock pulling a cart on an Indian village road, a porter lifting a suitcase at a railway station, or a milkman churning curd by hand. In every such case the body part (hand, leg, hoof) must physically touch the object for the force to act. Frictional force is the force that opposes the relative motion between two surfaces in contact; it acts at the surface where the two bodies touch, such as the friction between the tyres of a car and the road surface, between the brake pads and the wheel rim of a bicycle, or between the sole of a shoe and the ground when we walk. Because friction always arises at a surface of contact, it is firmly a contact force.

A non-contact force is one in which the two interacting bodies act on each other from a distance, without touching. The two important non-contact forces studied at this level are magnetic force and gravitational force. Magnetic force is the push or pull exerted by a magnet on magnetic materials such as iron, nickel, and cobalt; a bar magnet can attract an iron nail placed a few centimetres away, and a horseshoe magnet can pull a paperclip from a short distance without any contact. The Earth itself behaves like a giant magnet, which is why a freely suspended magnetic compass needle aligns along the north-south direction. Gravitational force is the force with which the Earth pulls every object towards its centre; it acts on objects even when they are far from the ground, which is why a ball thrown upwards slows down, stops, and falls back, and why a ripe mango drops from a tree branch in an Indian orchard. The gravitational force of the Earth also keeps the Moon in its orbit and is responsible for the weight of every body. The key distinction is therefore simple: if the force needs touch, it is a contact force; if the force acts across a distance, it is a non-contact force. Classifying forces in this way helps a student predict whether a particular force can act through empty space or only at a surface of contact, and it forms the framework on which later classes build the ideas of electrostatic force (Class 7) and nuclear forces (Class 8).
eli5: Some forces need you to touch the thing you are pushing or pulling -- like when you push a door or when your shoes grip the floor. These are contact forces. Other forces work from far away, like a magnet pulling a paperclip without touching it, or the Earth pulling a dropped ball down to the ground. These are non-contact forces. So the simple rule is: if it needs touch, it is contact; if it works from a distance, it is non-contact.

misconceptions.belief: Magnetic force is a contact force because the iron nail finally touches the magnet." This error mirrors the kind of confusion CISCE examiners repeatedly flag -- students confuse the cause of a force with its effect.
misconceptions.correction: The classification of a force depends on whether physical contact is required for the force to begin acting, not on whether the bodies touch after the force has pulled them together. A magnet attracts an iron nail from a distance before any contact occurs, so magnetic force is a non-contact force.

misconceptions.belief: Gravity is a contact force because the ball is touching the ground when it lands.
misconceptions.correction: Gravitational force acts on the ball throughout its flight -- while it is rising, at the highest point, and while it is falling -- even when nothing is touching it. The fact that the ball ends up touching the ground does not make gravity a contact force; gravity is a non-contact force because it acts across a distance.

misconceptions.belief: Friction is a non-contact force because it acts between two surfaces.
misconceptions.correction: Friction acts at the surface where two bodies are in contact. If the two surfaces are separated, friction disappears. Because physical contact between the two surfaces is essential, friction is a contact force.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Define contact force and non-contact force, and give one example of each.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: A contact force is a force that can act only when the two interacting bodies are in physical contact with each other -- that is, they must be touching. An example is muscular force, such as a boy pushing a heavy box across the floor, where his hands must press against the box for the push to act. Another example is frictional force, such as the friction between the tyres of a car and the road. A non-contact force is a force that acts on a body from a distance, without any physical contact between the two interacting bodies. An example is magnetic force, where a bar magnet attracts an iron nail placed a few centimetres away without touching it. Another example is gravitational force, where the Earth pulls a thrown ball back down even when the ball is high in the air and nothing is touching it. The key difference is whether physical contact is required for the force to act.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A horse pulls a cart along a road. Identify the two forces acting in this situation, classify each as contact or non-contact, and explain your classification.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: Two forces are acting in this situation. The first is the muscular force exerted by the horse on the cart through the harness and rope. This is a contact force because the horse's muscles produce the pull and the harness must be in physical contact with the cart for the force to be transmitted; if the rope breaks and contact is lost, the pull stops immediately. The second is the gravitational force exerted by the Earth on both the horse and the cart, pulling them downwards. This is a non-contact force because gravity acts on the horse and the cart even when they are moving along the road and nothing is touching them from below except the ground; the Earth pulls them towards its centre from a distance. A third force, frictional force between the cart's wheels and the road, is also present and is a contact force because it arises at the surface where the wheels touch the road. The reasoning in each case rests on a single test: does the force require the two bodies to touch, or can it act across a distance?

diagnosticQuestions.question: A student says, "A magnet picking up a pile of iron nails is an example of a contact force, because in the end the nails are stuck to the magnet and touching it." Evaluate this statement and give a balanced argument.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The student's statement is incorrect, although it contains a partial truth that must be carefully examined. The partial truth is that, after the force has acted, the iron nails do indeed end up in contact with the magnet and remain stuck to its surface. The student has observed this correctly. However, the error lies in using the final condition of the bodies -- the fact that they are touching after the event -- to classify the force. The correct test for classifying a force as contact or non-contact is to ask whether physical contact is required for the force to begin acting in the first place. In the case of a magnet and a pile of iron nails, the magnet begins to attract the nails while they are still lying on the table, several centimetres away and not touching the magnet at all. The nails then slide or jump across the gap and only afterwards come into contact with the magnet. Because the force was already acting before any contact occurred, magnetic force is classified as a non-contact force. If the student's reasoning were correct, then gravity would also have to be called a contact force, because a dropped ball ends up touching the ground -- yet gravity clearly acts on the ball throughout its fall, while it is still in the air and touching nothing. The same logic applies to the magnet: the end state of contact is a consequence of the force, not a requirement for the force to act. Therefore the student has confused the effect of the force with the condition needed for the force to operate. The correct classification is that magnetic force is a non-contact force, because it can act across a distance and does not require physical contact to begin acting. This distinction -- between "contact required to act" and "contact happens as a result" -- is exactly the kind of precision the ICSE board expects in a classification answer.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Classify each of the following forces as contact or non-contact, name the specific force, and give the reason: (a) a boy kicking a football, (b) a compass needle turning to point north, (c) a falling leaf from a neem tree, (d) a brake pad slowing a bicycle wheel.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: (a) A boy kicking a football is a contact force -- specifically muscular force -- because the boy's foot must physically touch the ball for the kick to act; if the foot does not meet the ball, no force is transmitted. (b) A compass needle turning to point north is a non-contact force -- specifically magnetic force -- because the Earth, behaving as a giant magnet, exerts a magnetic pull on the needle from a distance; the needle turns and aligns itself without anything touching it. (c) A falling leaf from a neem tree is a non-contact force -- specifically gravitational force -- because the Earth pulls the leaf downwards even while it is detached from the branch and falling through the air, with nothing in contact with it. (d) A brake pad slowing a bicycle wheel is a contact force -- specifically frictional force -- because the brake pad must press against the wheel rim, and the friction that slows the wheel arises only at the surface where the two are in contact; if the pad is pulled away, the braking force vanishes.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Design a simple classroom activity using four everyday objects that demonstrates one contact force and one non-contact force, and explain how you would use it to teach the difference to a Class 6 student.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: Take four everyday objects: a wooden block, a piece of string, a bar magnet, and a small iron nail. For the contact force demonstration, place the wooden block on a smooth table and ask a student to pull it across the table using the string tied around the block. The student will feel that the block moves only while the string is taut and in contact with the block; the moment the string goes slack or is released, the pull stops. Use this to teach that muscular force transmitted through the string is a contact force, because the pulling body and the block must be connected. For the non-contact force demonstration, place the iron nail on the table and slowly bring the bar magnet towards it from a few centimetres away, without letting them touch. The nail will suddenly slide towards the magnet and stick to it. Ask the student to observe that the nail began to move before any contact occurred. Use this to teach that magnetic force is a non-contact force, because the magnet acted on the nail across a gap. To consolidate the lesson, ask the student to state the single test that separates the two demonstrations: did the force need touch to start acting, or did it act from a distance? This hands-on comparison makes the abstract classification concrete and memorable for a Class 6 learner.

masteryCriteria: Can define a contact force as a force requiring physical contact between two bodies, and a non-contact force as a force that acts across a distance without contact. Can classify muscular force and frictional force as contact forces, and magnetic force and gravitational force as non-contact forces, giving the correct reason in each case. Can name two examples each of contact forces (e.g. a boy pushing a box -- muscular; brake pads on a wheel rim -- frictional) and non-contact forces (e.g. a magnet attracting an iron nail -- magnetic; the Earth pulling a falling mango -- gravitational). Can explain the difference between contact and non-contact forces using the single test of whether physical contact is required for the force to act.

title: Weight as the force of gravity on an object
subject: physics
definition:
Weight is the force with which the Earth pulls an object towards itself. It is not a separate kind of force but the gravitational force that the Earth exerts on every object lying on or near its surface. Because gravity is a non-contact force, it acts on an object continuously -- whether the object is resting on a table, falling through air, or being held in your hand -- without anything physically touching it. The Earth pulls every body vertically downward towards its centre, and this downward pull is what we call the weight of the body. Weight is a vector quantity because it has both magnitude and direction; the direction of weight is always towards the centre of the Earth.

Weight is closely related to mass. Mass is the quantity of matter contained in a body and is measured in kilograms (kg); it does not change from place to place because the amount of matter in an object stays the same. Weight, however, depends on how strongly the Earth (or any other celestial body) pulls that mass. The more mass an object has, the greater is the gravitational pull on it, and therefore the greater is its weight. So a 5 kg bag of rice has more weight than a 1 kg bag of rice because the Earth pulls the larger mass with a greater force. Although the formula W = mg is taught in Class 7, at this stage students must understand qualitatively that weight increases when mass increases, and that weight and mass are two different physical quantities.

The SI unit of weight is the newton, symbol N. One newton is a small unit -- roughly the weight of an object of mass 100 g, such as a medium-sized apple. A 1 kg object has a weight of about 10 N on the Earth. Weight, being a force, must always be expressed in newtons and never in kilograms, because kilograms measure mass, not force. This distinction is one of the most important ideas in this node.

Weight is measured using a spring balance. A spring balance contains a coiled spring fixed at its top end; when a body is hung from the hook at the lower end, the spring stretches. The more weight the body has, the more the spring stretches. A pointer attached to the spring moves over a graduated scale marked in newtons, and the reading gives the weight of the body directly. A spring balance therefore measures weight (force), not mass. The same object weighed on a spring balance on the Moon would show a smaller reading because the Moon's gravitational pull is weaker than the Earth's, even though the object's mass has not changed. This shows clearly that weight depends on the gravitational force of the body doing the pulling, while mass is an intrinsic property of the object.
eli5: Weight is the invisible tug the Earth gives every object to pull it down. The more stuff (mass) an object has, the harder the Earth tugs, so the heavier it feels. Weight is measured in newtons using a spring balance, which stretches more when the tug is stronger. On the Moon the tug is weaker, so you feel lighter -- but you still have the same amount of stuff inside you.

misconceptions.belief: Weight and mass are the same thing, and both are measured in kilograms." This is the most common error and is exactly the kind of confusion CISCE examiners flagged in the 2025 PPA when they noted that "many candidates answered incorrectly due to lack of clarity regarding the fundamentals of vectors and scalars" -- mass is a scalar (just a quantity of matter, in kg), while weight is a force (a vector, in N).
misconceptions.correction: Mass is the amount of matter in a body, measured in kilograms, and is constant everywhere. Weight is the gravitational force with which the Earth pulls that mass, measured in newtons, and it changes from place to place because gravity changes.

misconceptions.belief: Weight stays the same everywhere -- on the Earth, on the Moon, in space.
misconceptions.correction: Weight depends on the gravitational pull of the body doing the attracting. The Moon's gravity is about one-sixth of the Earth's, so the same object weighs about one-sixth as much on the Moon. Mass stays the same, but weight does not. This is why a spring balance gives different readings on the Earth and the Moon for the same object.

misconceptions.belief: A spring balance measures mass.
misconceptions.correction: A spring balance measures weight (force), because it works by the stretching of a spring under the gravitational pull on the hung body. A physical balance (or beam balance) compares masses and measures mass. Confusing the two instruments leads to wrong answers in board questions that ask which instrument measures weight.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Define weight and state its SI unit. Name the instrument used to measure weight.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: Weight is the force with which the Earth pulls an object towards itself. It is the gravitational force exerted by the Earth on a body, and its direction is always vertically downward, towards the centre of the Earth. Because weight is a force, its SI unit is the newton, symbol N. One newton is roughly the weight of a 100 g object such as a medium apple, and a 1 kg object weighs about 10 N on the Earth. The instrument used to measure weight is a spring balance. A spring balance has a coiled spring with a hook; when a body is hung from the hook, the spring stretches in proportion to the gravitational pull on the body, and a pointer on a graduated scale marked in newtons gives the weight directly. It is important to remember that a spring balance measures weight (a force), not mass.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Explain why the weight of an astronaut changes when she goes from the Earth to the Moon, even though her mass does not change.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: Mass is the quantity of matter contained in a body and is an intrinsic property of that body -- it does not depend on where the body is located. So the astronaut's mass stays the same on the Earth and on the Moon. Weight, however, is the gravitational force with which a celestial body pulls that mass. The Earth is much more massive than the Moon, so the Earth's gravitational pull is much stronger -- about six times stronger. Because the Moon pulls the same mass with a much smaller force, the astronaut's weight on the Moon is only about one-sixth of her weight on the Earth. This is why astronauts appear to "float" or feel very light on the Moon. The example shows clearly that weight depends on the gravitational force of the attracting body, while mass is independent of it. If she used a spring balance on the Moon, it would show a smaller reading in newtons, but a beam balance comparing her mass against standard masses would give the same mass in kilograms.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A student writes, "A 2 kg bag of sugar has a weight of 2 kg, and this weight is the same on the Earth and on the Moon." Evaluate the correctness of this statement.
diagnosticQuestions.answer:
The statement is incorrect on two counts. First, the student confuses the unit of mass with the unit of weight. The 2 kg refers to the mass of the bag -- the quantity of matter it contains -- and mass is correctly measured in kilograms. Weight, however, is a force, and force is measured in newtons (N), not in kilograms. On the Earth, a 2 kg mass has a weight of about 20 N (using the rough relation that 1 kg weighs about 10 N on Earth). Writing "weight = 2 kg" is therefore a category error: it attaches a mass unit to a force quantity. This is exactly the kind of confusion CISCE examiners warned about in the 2025 PPA when they noted candidates' "lack of clarity regarding the fundamentals of vectors and scalars" -- mass is a scalar in kg, weight is a force (a vector) in N.

Second, the student claims the weight is the same on the Earth and the Moon. This is also wrong. Weight depends on the gravitational pull of the attracting body. The Moon's gravitational pull is only about one-sixth of the Earth's, so the same 2 kg bag would weigh only about one-sixth as much on the Moon (roughly 3 to 4 N). The mass of the bag -- 2 kg -- does stay the same on both bodies, because mass is the amount of matter and does not depend on gravity. So the correct statement would be: "A 2 kg bag of sugar has a mass of 2 kg, which is the same on the Earth and the Moon; on the Earth its weight is about 20 N, and on the Moon its weight is about one-sixth of that." The student's error lies in treating mass and weight as identical and in ignoring that weight depends on the local gravitational force.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A spring balance shows a reading of 15 N when a body is hung from it on the Earth. Explain what the reading tells you, and predict roughly what the same spring balance would show if the body were taken to the Moon. State which quantity of the body stays unchanged.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The reading of 15 N tells us the weight of the body on the Earth -- that is, the gravitational force with which the Earth is pulling the body is 15 newtons. Because the spring balance works by the stretching of its spring under the gravitational pull, the reading is a direct measure of weight (a force), not of mass. Since the Moon's gravity is about one-sixth of the Earth's gravity, the same body would be pulled with about one-sixth of the force on the Moon. So the spring balance would show roughly 15 / 6, which is about 2.5 N, on the Moon. The quantity that stays unchanged is the mass of the body -- the amount of matter in it does not depend on where it is. This is why we say mass is constant but weight is not: the spring balance reading changes because the gravitational pull changes, even though the body itself has not lost or gained any matter.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Design a simple classroom activity using a spring balance, a 1 kg mass, and a 2 kg mass to demonstrate the relationship between mass and weight. Describe what students would observe and what conclusion they should draw.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: Hang the spring balance from a fixed support so that it hangs vertically with the pointer at the zero mark. First attach the 1 kg mass to the hook and let it hang freely. Ask students to note the reading on the newton scale -- it will be about 10 N. Now remove the 1 kg mass and hang the 2 kg mass from the same hook. Students will observe that the pointer moves further down and the reading is now about 20 N, roughly double the first reading. They should also notice that the spring stretched more for the heavier body, showing visually that a greater gravitational pull produces a greater stretch. From these two observations students should conclude that weight increases when mass increases -- the 2 kg mass, having twice the matter, is pulled twice as hard by the Earth and therefore has twice the weight. They should also record that the unit on the scale is newtons, confirming that the spring balance measures weight (a force) and not mass. As an extension, the teacher can ask students to predict what the reading would be on the Moon (about one-sixth) to reinforce that weight depends on gravity while mass does not.

masteryCriteria: Can define weight as the force with which the Earth pulls an object towards itself, and state that its direction is vertically downward; can state the SI unit of weight as the newton (N) and give a feel for its size (1 kg weighs about 10 N on Earth, 100 g weighs about 1 N); can name the spring balance as the instrument that measures weight and explain that it works by the stretching of a spring under gravitational pull; can distinguish mass (quantity of matter in kg, constant everywhere) from weight (gravitational force in N, changes with gravity such as on the Moon).

title: Pressure as force per unit area
subject: physics
definition: Pressure is defined as the force acting normally (perpendicularly) on a surface divided by the area over which that force is distributed. In symbols, pressure = force / area, written as P = F / A. The SI unit of force is the newton (N) and the SI unit of area is the square metre (m^2), so the SI unit of pressure is the newton per square metre (N/m^2), which is given the special name pascal (Pa) in honour of the French scientist Blaise Pascal. One pascal is therefore a very small pressure -- it is the pressure produced by a force of one newton acting on an area of one square metre. Because pressure depends on two quantities (force and area), it can be increased in two ways: by increasing the force while keeping the area the same, or by decreasing the area while keeping the force the same. Conversely, pressure can be reduced by decreasing the force or by increasing the area. This is why a sharp knife cuts better than a blunt one -- the same pushing force is concentrated over the very small area of the fine edge, producing a large pressure that easily separates the material. A blunt knife has a wider edge, so the same force spreads over a larger area and produces less pressure. The same principle explains why a needle pierces cloth easily while a finger pressing with the same force does not -- the needle's tip has a tiny area. It also explains why school bags have broad straps: the weight of the bag (a force) is spread over a larger area of the shoulder, reducing the pressure and the pain. Buildings are constructed with broad, heavy foundations so the enormous weight of the structure is distributed over a large area of ground, keeping the pressure on the soil low and preventing the building from sinking. A person standing on soft snow in ordinary boots sinks because body weight acts on the small area of the boot soles; the same person wearing skis or snowshoes does not sink because the wide skis spread the weight over a much larger area. Lying on a bed of nails works on the same idea -- the body's weight is distributed over hundreds of nail points, so the pressure at any one point is small enough to be safe. Pressure is thus a measure of how concentrated a force is over a surface, and understanding it lets us explain a wide range of everyday situations in which the same force can feel very different depending on the area over which it acts.
eli5: Imagine pressing a pencil tip and the flat back of the pencil into your hand with the same push. The tip hurts because the same push is squeezed onto a tiny spot -- that is high pressure. The flat back feels gentle because the push is spread over a big spot -- that is low pressure. Pressure is just how concentrated a force is on a surface. Big force or small area means high pressure; small force or big area means low pressure.

misconceptions.belief: A sharp knife cuts better because it has more force.
misconceptions.correction: The force from your hand is the same whether the knife is sharp or blunt. The sharp knife cuts better because its edge has a much smaller area, so the same force produces a much larger pressure (P = F / A). It is the pressure, not the force, that does the cutting. CISCE examiners note that many candidates "answered by guesswork" and were "not clear with the concept" -- confusing force with pressure is a classic example. Always identify whether the question is about force or about pressure.

misconceptions.belief: Pressure and force are the same thing.
misconceptions.correction: Force is a push or pull measured in newtons (N); pressure is force divided by area measured in pascal (Pa). Two situations can have the same force but very different pressure if the areas differ. Examiners repeatedly insist that students "express every physical quantity with proper unit" -- writing N when you mean Pa (or vice versa) shows this confusion and loses marks.

misconceptions.belief: Increasing the area always increases the pressure.
misconceptions.correction: It is the opposite. For a fixed force, increasing the area decreases the pressure (P = F / A). This is why broad straps and wide skis reduce pressure. Students who invert the formula give backwards explanations for everyday examples.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Define pressure and state its SI unit.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: Pressure is the force acting normally (perpendicularly) on a surface per unit area of that surface. It is defined by the formula P = F / A, where P is pressure, F is the force in newtons, and A is the area in square metres over which the force is distributed. The SI unit of pressure is the pascal (Pa), which is equal to one newton per square metre (1 Pa = 1 N/m^2). Pressure tells us how concentrated a force is over a surface: a large force on a small area gives a high pressure, while the same force on a large area gives a low pressure. For example, a force of 10 N acting on 2 m^2 gives a pressure of 5 Pa. Always write the unit (Pa) with the numerical answer, as CISCE examiners expect every physical quantity to carry its proper unit.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Explain why a sharp knife cuts better than a blunt one using the concept of pressure.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: When you press a knife down on a vegetable, your hand applies a certain force -- say 20 N -- regardless of whether the knife is sharp or blunt. What differs is the area of the cutting edge. A sharp knife has a very thin edge with a tiny area, perhaps 0.0001 m^2, so the pressure is P = F / A = 20 / 0.0001 = 200,000 Pa. A blunt knife has a thicker, wider edge, perhaps 0.001 m^2, so the pressure is only 20 / 0.001 = 20,000 Pa -- ten times smaller. Because pressure measures how concentrated the force is, the sharp knife concentrates the same push onto a far smaller area, producing enough pressure to separate the fibres of the material and cut through it. The blunt knife spreads the same push over a larger area, producing less pressure, so it merely squashes rather than cuts. Thus the sharpness works through area, not through extra force.
