When you press two sheets of sandpaper harder together, the irregularities are forced more deeply into each other, the interlocking becomes stronger, and friction increases. When the pressing force is reduced, the interlocking loosens and friction decreases. Thus, a heavier block pulled along a table experiences more friction than a lighter block made of the same material, because the heavier block presses down on the table with a greater normal force.

Friction is not always a nuisance. It is essential for walking, braking, holding objects, and lighting a match. To reduce friction where it is harmful, we use lubrication (oil or grease between moving parts), polish surfaces, use wheels or ball bearings to convert sliding friction into the smaller rolling friction, or streamline shapes. The classic Class 7 activity uses a spring balance to pull a wooden block across sandpaper, glass, and wood, measuring the frictional force in each case and confirming that rougher surfaces give higher spring-balance readings and that adding a weight on top of the block (increasing normal force) raises the reading further.
eli5: Imagine two pieces of sandpaper rubbing on each other. Their tiny bumps catch like the hooks of Velcro, and that catching is friction -- a force that tries to stop the sliding. Rougher paper has bigger bumps, so it catches more and friction is bigger. Now press the two sheets harder together and the bumps sink deeper into each other, so it is even harder to slide them -- that is the normal force making friction bigger. Smooth glass has almost no bumps, so it slides easily. That is all friction is: bumps catching, and how hard you press them together.

misconceptions.belief: Friction always acts opposite to the direction of motion of the body.
misconceptions.correction: Friction acts opposite to the direction of relative motion (or tendency of relative motion) between the two surfaces in contact, not necessarily opposite to the body's motion. When you walk forward, your foot pushes backward on the road; the friction on your foot acts forward -- in the same direction as your body's motion -- because it opposes the backward tendency of your foot relative to the ground. This is exactly the kind of conceptual confusion CISCE examiners flagged in the 2024 and 2025 PPA under vector-direction errors (candidates "applied incorrect logic" and confused direction of force with direction of motion). Always think: friction opposes relative sliding of the contact surfaces, not the body's travel.

misconceptions.belief: Heavier objects always have more friction because they are heavier.
misconceptions.correction: It is not weight as such but the normal force -- the perpendicular force pressing the surfaces together -- that determines friction. On a horizontal surface the normal force happens to equal the weight, so a heavier block does show more friction. But on an inclined plane the normal force is less than the weight (it equals mg cos theta), so the same heavy block presses the plane less hard and friction is smaller than its weight would suggest. The correct statement is: friction increases when the normal force increases, and on a horizontal surface that means a heavier object shows more friction. Examiners in the PPA repeatedly remind students to "express every physical quantity with proper unit" and to be precise -- saying "normal force" instead of "weight" is the precise formulation that earns marks.

misconceptions.belief: Smooth surfaces have no friction.
misconceptions.correction: Even highly polished surfaces show some friction because no surface is perfectly smooth at the microscopic level -- irregularities always exist, and inter-molecular attraction at the contact also contributes. Friction can be made very small by polishing, lubrication, or using rolling bearings, but it cannot be reduced to zero in ordinary situations. A good example is ice: it seems frictionless, yet an ice skater does slide to a stop eventually. So the correct statement is "smooth surfaces have less friction than rough ones," not "no friction."

diagnosticQuestions.question: Define friction and name the two main factors that affect its magnitude.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: Friction is a contact force that opposes the relative motion (or the tendency of relative motion) between two surfaces in contact. It arises because the microscopic irregularities -- tiny hills and valleys -- on the two surfaces interlock when the surfaces are pressed together, and a force is needed to shear these interlocked bumps. The two main factors that affect the magnitude of friction are: (1) the nature or roughness of the surfaces in contact -- rougher surfaces have larger irregularities that interlock more deeply, giving greater friction, while smoother surfaces have smaller irregularities and give less friction; and (2) the normal force, that is, the force with which the two surfaces are pressed together perpendicular to the surface of contact. On a horizontal surface the normal force is equal to the weight of the body, so a heavier body presses down harder, the irregularities interlock more tightly, and friction is greater. Both factors act in the same direction: increasing either surface roughness or normal force increases friction, and decreasing either reduces friction. Examples include the high friction of sandpaper compared with glass, and the increase in friction when a weight is placed on a block being dragged with a spring balance.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A wooden block is pulled at constant speed across a sandpaper sheet and the spring balance reads 4 N. The same block is then pulled across a glass sheet and the reading is 1.5 N. Explain, in terms of surface irregularities, why the readings differ, and predict what will happen to the sandpaper reading if a 1 kg mass is placed on the block.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The spring-balance reading at constant speed equals the frictional force, because at constant velocity the applied pull and the friction are equal and opposite. Sandpaper is a rough surface with large, numerous irregularities -- tall hills and deep valleys -- so when the wooden block rests on it, the bumps of the block and the bumps of the sandpaper interlock deeply. To keep the block sliding, the pull must overcome this strong interlocking, so the reading is high (4 N). Glass, by contrast, is a very smooth surface with tiny, shallow irregularities; the interlocking with the block is weak, so only a small pull is needed and the reading is low (1.5 N). The difference in the two readings is therefore due to the first factor affecting friction -- the nature or roughness of the surfaces. If a 1 kg mass is placed on the block, the normal force increases by about 10 N (since 1 kg weighs roughly 10 N). This greater pressing force drives the irregularities of the block and the sandpaper more deeply into each other, tightening the interlock. As a result the frictional force rises, and the spring-balance reading needed to maintain constant speed will increase -- it might rise to around 6-8 N depending on the surfaces. This demonstrates the second factor: friction increases when the normal force increases.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A student says, "Friction is always a disadvantage, so we should try to remove it completely from all situations." Evaluate this statement, giving a balanced argument with at least two examples where friction is useful and two where it is harmful, and state whether the student is correct.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The student's statement is incorrect because it treats friction as universally harmful, whereas friction is both a help and a hindrance depending on the situation. A balanced view must weigh both sides. On the useful side, friction is essential for walking: when we push our foot backward against the road, friction acts forward on the foot and propels us; without friction we would slip and fall, exactly as happens on a wet, polished marble floor. Friction is also essential for braking -- the brake pads of a bicycle or car grip the wheel rim or disc because of friction, and tyres grip the road because of friction; remove it and vehicles could not stop. Other useful examples include writing with chalk on a blackboard, holding a glass without it slipping, and striking a match (friction generates the heat that ignites the chemicals). On the harmful side, friction between moving parts of machinery causes wear and tear and produces unwanted heat, wasting energy and reducing efficiency -- this is why oil or grease (lubrication) is used in engine parts, bicycle axles, and ceiling-fan bearings. Friction also opposes motion in vehicles, raising fuel consumption, and it heats up tyres on long drives. So the correct position is not to "remove friction completely" but to manage it: increase friction where it is useful (rough shoe soles, tyre treads, brake pads) and reduce it where it is harmful (lubrication, polishing, ball bearings, streamlining). The student has over-generalised; friction is a double-edged force, and a competent student must distinguish the contexts in which it should be maximised from those in which it should be minimised. Therefore the statement is false as written.

diagnosticQuestions.question: You are given a wooden block, a spring balance, a sheet of sandpaper, a glass plate, and a 1 kg weight. Describe step-by-step how you would perform an activity to show that (a) roughness of the surface affects friction, and (b) normal force affects friction. State what readings you would compare and what result you would expect.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: First, hook the spring balance to the wooden block and place the block on the sandpaper sheet on a flat table. Pull the spring balance horizontally and slowly so that the block moves at a steady (constant) speed; read and note the value on the spring balance -- call it R1. Because the speed is constant, the applied pull equals the frictional force, so R1 is the friction on sandpaper. Next, place the same block on the glass plate and again pull horizontally at constant speed; note the reading as R2. Comparing R1 and R2 shows the effect of surface roughness: R1 (sandpaper) should be clearly larger than R2 (glass), because sandpaper is rougher and its irregularities interlock more strongly with the block. This demonstrates factor (a). For factor (b), return the block to the sandpaper sheet and now place the 1 kg weight on top of the block, so the normal force increases by about 10 N. Pull horizontally at constant speed and note the reading as R3. Compare R3 with R1: R3 should be larger than R1 because the added weight has pressed the surfaces together more firmly, driving the irregularities deeper and raising friction. To make the activity fair, keep the same block, the same sandpaper area, and the same pulling speed in each comparison, and repeat each reading two or three times to take an average. The expected conclusion is that friction increases with surface roughness (R1 > R2) and with normal force (R3 > R1), confirming both factors.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Design a simple device or method that a cyclist in a hilly Indian town like Mussoorie could use to (i) increase friction when going downhill for safety, and (ii) reduce friction on the chain and axle for an easier ride. Explain the science behind each of your two choices using the factors affecting friction.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: For (i) increasing friction downhill, I would fit the bicycle with tyres that have deep, bold treads and, in the wet monsoon season, with ribbed or studded rubber tyres, and I would advise the rider to apply the brakes gently and intermittently using rubber brake pads that press hard on the metal rim. The science: deep treads make the tyre surface rougher, so the irregularities of the rubber interlock more strongly with the irregularities of the wet, slippery road surface -- this is the surface-roughness factor increasing friction and giving better grip on the steep Mussoorie slopes. Pressing the brake pads firmly against the rim increases the normal force between pad and rim, so by the normal-force factor the friction rises and the braking effect is stronger, letting the rider descend safely at a controlled speed. For (ii) reducing friction on the chain and axle, I would apply a few drops of bicycle oil (a lubricant) to the chain links and pack the wheel hubs with grease and ball bearings. The science: oil and grease form a thin film between the metal surfaces of the chain links and the axle, filling in the microscopic irregularities so the metal surfaces do not touch directly -- this reduces the effective roughness and therefore reduces friction (the lubrication factor). Ball bearings convert sliding friction between the axle and the hub into rolling friction, which is much smaller because rolling irregularities interlock far less than sliding ones. Together, lubrication and ball bearings reduce the friction that wastes the rider's effort, making the long climb up the hill easier and saving energy. Thus the same two factors -- surface roughness and normal force -- are manipulated in opposite directions: increased for safety (grip and braking) and decreased for efficiency (chain and axle).

masteryCriteria: Can define friction as a contact force that opposes the relative motion (or tendency of motion) between two surfaces in contact; can name the two factors affecting friction -- surface roughness and normal force -- and state that rougher surfaces and greater normal force increase friction while smoother surfaces and lower normal force reduce it; can explain each factor in terms of interlocking of surface irregularities (e.g., sandpaper gives a higher spring-balance reading than glass; a 1 kg weight added to a block raises the reading by increasing normal force by about 10 N); can give one daily-life example of increasing friction (tyre treads, brake pads) and one of reducing friction (lubrication, ball bearings).

title: Turning effect of force (moment of force)
subject: physics
definition:
The moment of a force is the turning effect produced by a force about a fixed point called the pivot (or fulcrum, or axis of rotation). When a force is applied to a body that is not acting through the pivot, it tends to rotate the body either clockwise or anticlockwise about that pivot. The magnitude of this turning effect is given by the formula: moment of force = force x perpendicular distance from the pivot, written as M = F x d, where F is the applied force in newtons (N) and d is the perpendicular distance from the line of action of the force to the pivot, measured in metres (m). The SI unit of moment of force is the newton-metre (Nxm). In CGS units it is measured in dyne-centimetre (dyn cm), and the conversion is 1 Nxm = 10^7 dyn cm, or equivalently 1 dyn cm = 10^-7 Nxm.

The perpendicular distance is the shortest distance from the pivot to the line along which the force acts -- it is not simply the distance from the pivot to the point where the force is applied unless the force acts at right angles to that line. This distinction is crucial: the same force produces a larger moment when applied farther from the pivot and at right angles to the lever arm. Everyday examples include opening a door by pushing on the handle (placed far from the hinge so a small force suffices), turning a tap, and using a spanner with a long handle to loosen a tight bolt -- in each case, increasing the perpendicular distance reduces the force needed for the same turning effect.

The principle of moments states that when a body is in rotational equilibrium about a pivot, the sum of the clockwise moments about the pivot equals the sum of the anticlockwise moments. This is the basis of the beam balance, the see-saw, and the lever. For example, on a see-saw a heavier child sitting closer to the pivot can balance a lighter child sitting farther away, because W1 x d1 = W2 x d2. Numerical problems require calculating the moment given F and d, or finding an unknown force or distance by applying the principle of moments. The direction of the moment (clockwise or anticlockwise) is determined by observing the sense of rotation the force would produce about the pivot.
eli5: Imagine a seesaw. The pivot is the middle point that doesn't move. If you push down far from the pivot, the seesaw turns easily; if you push close to it, turning is hard. The "moment" is just a number that tells you how strong this turning effect is: multiply your push (force) by how far from the pivot you pushed (perpendicular distance). Bigger force or bigger distance means a bigger turn. Its unit is Nxm.

misconceptions.belief: Students treat "perpendicular distance" as the distance from the pivot to the point where the force is applied.
misconceptions.correction: Perpendicular distance is the shortest distance from the pivot to the line of action of the force. If the force is not applied at right angles to the line joining pivot to the point of application, the perpendicular distance is smaller than that geometric distance, and the moment is F x (perpendicular distance), not F x (slant distance).

diagnosticQuestions.question: Define moment of force, state its SI unit, and give the relation between its SI and CGS units.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: Moment of force is the turning effect of a force about an axis of rotation (or fulcrum). It is equal to the product of the force and the perpendicular distance from the axis of rotation to the line of action of the force, i.e. M = F x d, where F is the force in newton and d is the perpendicular distance in metre. The SI unit of moment of force is the newton-metre (Nxm). The CGS unit is the dyne-centimetre (dyn cm). The relation between them is 1 Nxm = 10^7 dyn cm, or equivalently 1 dyn cm = 10^-7 Nxm. This conversion follows because 1 N = 10^5 dyn and 1 m = 10^2 cm, so 1 Nxm = 10^5 x 10^2 = 10^7 dyn cm. Examiners have repeatedly stressed that the definition must mention the axis of rotation/fulcrum and the perpendicular distance to the line of action -- omitting these costs marks.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A force of 20 N is applied to a spanner 25 cm long at right angles to its handle. Calculate the moment produced. Explain why a longer spanner makes it easier to loosen a tight bolt.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: First convert the length to metres: 25 cm = 0.25 m. Since the force is applied at right angles to the handle, the perpendicular distance from the pivot (the bolt at the centre) to the line of action of the force equals the length of the spanner, 0.25 m. Moment = force x perpendicular distance = 20 N x 0.25 m = 5 Nxm, and the sense of rotation is clockwise (or anticlockwise, depending on the direction of push). A longer spanner makes loosening easier because moment = F x d -- for the same applied force F, a larger perpendicular distance d gives a larger moment, so the turning effect on the bolt is greater. Equivalently, to produce the same moment needed to overcome a tight bolt, a longer d means a smaller F is required, so the mechanic's hand needs to push less hard. This is the lever principle in action: increasing the lever arm trades distance for force.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A student states: "For a body to be in equilibrium under the principle of moments, the fulcrum must always be at the centre of the body." Evaluate this statement with reference to a loaded ruler balanced on a knife-edge.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The statement is incorrect. Equilibrium under the principle of moments requires only that the sum of clockwise moments about the pivot equals the sum of anticlockwise moments about that pivot -- it does not require the fulcrum to be at the geometric centre of the body. Consider a uniform ruler of weight W_r (acting at its centre of mass, the 50 cm mark) balanced on a knife-edge with a weight W1 hung at one end and W2 hung at the other. If W1 is heavier than W2, the knife-edge (fulcrum) must be placed closer to W1 and farther from W2 so that W1 x d1 (clockwise) equals W2 x d2 plus the ruler's own moment (anticlockwise or clockwise depending on which side of the fulcrum the centre of mass lies). The fulcrum's correct position is dictated by the equality of moments, not by the midpoint of the ruler. The CISCE 2025 examiner report explicitly noted that many candidates failed to grasp that the fulcrum is closer to the larger weight and away from the smaller weight, and that they neglected the moment due to the ruler's own weight. A balanced argument: in the special case where equal weights hang at equal distances on a uniform ruler and the ruler's weight is negligible or acts at the pivot, the fulcrum does coincide with the centre -- but this is a special case, not a general rule. In general, the fulcrum shifts away from the centre to satisfy the moment equation, and the weight of the ruler itself, acting at its centre of mass, contributes an additional moment that must be included. Therefore the student's claim is false as a general statement; equilibrium is about balanced moments, not about a centred fulcrum.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A uniform metre rule of weight 0.5 N is balanced on a knife-edge at the 40 cm mark. A weight of 2 N is hung at the 10 cm mark. Where should a 1.5 N weight be hung on the other side for the rule to remain horizontal?
diagnosticQuestions.answer: Take moments about the knife-edge at the 40 cm mark. The 2 N weight is at 10 cm, so its perpendicular distance from the pivot is 40 - 10 = 30 cm = 0.30 m, producing a clockwise moment = 2 x 0.30 = 0.60 Nxm. The ruler's own weight 0.5 N acts at its centre of mass, the 50 cm mark, which is 50 - 40 = 10 cm = 0.10 m to the other side of the pivot, producing an anticlockwise moment = 0.5 x 0.10 = 0.05 Nxm. Let the 1.5 N weight be hung at the x cm mark on the anticlockwise side (x > 40). Its distance from the pivot is (x - 40) cm = (x - 40)/100 m, and its anticlockwise moment = 1.5 x (x - 40)/100. For equilibrium, clockwise moment = total anticlockwise moment: 0.60 = 0.05 + 1.5 x (x - 40)/100. So 1.5 x (x - 40)/100 = 0.55, giving (x - 40)/100 = 0.55/1.5 = 0.3667, so x - 40 = 36.67, hence x ~= 76.67 cm. The 1.5 N weight should be hung at approximately the 76.7 cm mark. This problem illustrates the examiner's 2025 point: the ruler's own weight contributes a moment and must not be neglected.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Design a simple experiment using a metre rule, a knife-edge, and two known slotted weights to verify the principle of moments. Describe the procedure, the measurements, and how you would check the principle.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: Take a uniform metre rule and balance it on a knife-edge to find its centre of mass (for a uniform rule this is the 50 cm mark); record the rule's weight using a spring balance. Now shift the knife-edge to an arbitrary mark, say the 30 cm mark, so the rule's centre of mass (50 cm) is 20 cm to one side, producing a known moment due to the rule's own weight. Hang a slotted weight W1 (say 1 N) at the 10 cm mark on the same side as the centre of mass; its distance from the pivot is 30 - 10 = 20 cm. On the other side, hang a second slotted weight W2 (say 2 N) and slide it along the rule until the rule balances horizontally; record its position, say x cm. Measure the perpendicular distances d1 and d2 of W1 and W2 from the knife-edge, and the distance dr of the rule's centre of mass from the knife-edge. Compute the total clockwise moment = W1 x d1 + Wr x dr (whichever side is clockwise) and the anticlockwise moment = W2 x d2. If the two totals are equal within experimental error, the principle of moments is verified. Repeat with different weights and different pivot positions to confirm consistency. Sources of error include the rule not being perfectly uniform, friction at the knife-edge, and reading the scale at an angle (parallax). This experiment directly mirrors the kind of question CISCE examiners set, where candidates must draw forces at the ends of the scale, mark the fulcrum correctly, and include the moment due to the rule's own weight.

masteryCriteria: Can define moment of force as the turning effect of a force about an axis of rotation (or fulcrum), equal to force x perpendicular distance from the axis of rotation to the line of action of the force; Can calculate moment using M = F x d with correct unit Nxm (e.g. 20 N at 0.25 m gives 5 Nxm) and convert between SI and CGS units (1 Nxm = 10^7 dyn cm); Can apply the principle of moments (sum of clockwise moments = sum of anticlockwise moments) to find an unknown force or distance, including the moment due to the weight of the ruler acting at its centre of mass; Can identify the sense of rotation (clockwise or anticlockwise) of a force about a given pivot.
